targets.approach: Shares the same remote, multi-day approach as the peak's northwest-couloir route: via Hannegan Pass Trail and Whatcom/Perfect Pass to the Challenger Glacier and West Challenger Notch, descending to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier below the peak's north/east side (or via the alternate Big Beaver Trailhead-Wiley Ridge-Challenger Arm approach).
targets.descent: not recorded; presumed to reverse the east face or descend via the adjacent northwest-couloir line back to the glacier.

targets.approach: Western approach (the recommended option): roughly 10 miles with about 7,800 ft of gain via the Ptarmigan Traverse trail toward Spire Point — described as a 'brutal approach' with significant bushwhacking. wa_chair_bryant_traverse.approach: Begins on Chair Peak's north ridge, reached via the East Face/Northeast Buttress approach (Alpental parking, Snow Lake Trail, Source Lake fork, then a gully to roughly 4,800 ft and the basin below), then continues along the crest over/past Bryant Peak.
wa_chair_bryant_traverse.descent_text: Typically descend from wherever the traverse is exited (Bryant, the Tooth, or Denny) via that peak's own standard descent, since reversing the ridge crest is slow and exposed.
wa_chair_bryant_traverse.name: Chair-Bryant Traverse

wa_chair_peak_east_face.approach: From the Alpental parking lot, take the Snow Lake Trail; at about 1.5 miles turn off toward Source Lake. Ascend a 3rd-class rocky gully starting around 4,200 ft, reach a small cliff around 4,800 ft, traverse through a notch, then cross a snowy basin to the base of the route around 5,500 ft.
wa_chair_peak_east_face.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb and traverse back toward the notch area, locate the marked south-facing rappel gully (the southern chimney), and make two single-rope rappels down the chimney and a third down the steep, narrow snow finger below it to return to the approach basin.
wa_chair_peak_east_face.name: East Face

wa_chair_peak_north_face.approach: Park at the upper Alpental parking lot (end of Alpental Road, shared with the Snow Lake / Source Lake trailhead). Pick up the maintained Alpental Valley trail, which runs along and above the South Fork Snoqualmie River on the old ski-area service road/cat track for about the first 0.5 mile before narrowing to a standard trail. Continue up-valley roughly 1.5-2 miles, climbing gently through forest and avalanche-path brush with Chair Peak's north side visible ahead; a boot path forks off the main Source Lake/Snow Lake trail toward Source Lake and the basin below Chair Peak's east/north aspect (~4200 ft). From the basin, ascend talus and (in season) a snow apron directly toward the base of the north face at the head of the Alpental cirque, aiming for the obvious snow/ice runnel system below the summit block. Total approach gain to the base is roughly 2,400 ft over about 2.5-3 miles one-way. Hazards: the valley floor and lower slopes cross active avalanche paths below Chair Peak, Snoqualmie Mountain, and The Tooth, so this is a serious slide-prone approach in winter/spring — most parties go early and move quickly through the runout zones; there is also a creek crossing near Source Lake
wa_chair_peak_north_face.descent_text: From the summit, most parties reverse toward the notch/col below the summit block and descend the gully on the south side of the east face (sometimes described as the same gully used by the Northeast Buttress descent). Expect a mix of downclimbing and rappelling: parties commonly do two double-rope (60m) rappels — the first from trees/rock anchors near the head of the gully with some downclimbing to reach the next station, and a second double-rope rappel that reaches easier snow near the gully's base — though some parties describe reaching the base with a single 60m rappel plus downclimbing depending on snow coverage. Anchors are a mix of natural gear (trees, rock horns/slings) rather than bolts; bring cord/webbing to back up or replace tattered slings. From the base of the gully, downclimb snow/talus east back into the Chair Peak basin and pick up the approach trail to Source Lake and out. Watch for cornices at the gully lip early season, loose rock in the gully when snow-free, and wet-slide hazard on the descent slopes during warm spring conditions.
wa_chair_peak_north_face.name: North Face

wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.approach: From the upper Alpental parking lot (I-90 Exit 52, end of Alpental Road), follow the Alpental Valley/Source Lake trail: the first 0.5 mile follows the old ski-area cat track, then it becomes a standard trail climbing gently through forest for about 0.75 mile to Source Lake (roughly 1.25-1.75 miles and a few hundred feet of gain from the car). From Source Lake, leave the maintained trail and head cross-country/up boot path toward the basin below Chair Peak's east face (~4200 ft), a further 0.5-1 mile with steeper talus, heather, and (early/mid season) snow slopes. From the basin, climb a short snow gully for approximately 300 ft to gain the crest of the ridge that forms the Northeast Buttress, then follow the ridge to the start of the technical climbing. Total approach is on the order of 2-2.5 miles and 1,700-2,000 ft of gain one-way to the base of the buttress. Hazards: the basin and approach gully sit below avalanche terrain off Chair Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain — this is a classic early-season slide path, and parties often describe deep postholing, wet-slab activity, and wind-loaded slopes here; a rope/axe/crampons are typically carried from the basin onward given the exposure o
wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.descent_text:
From the top of the buttress, scramble back across the flat summit area and drop into the first obvious gully on climber's left — not the gully further along the ridge near the true summit. Old tat on two small trees marks the entrance. The gully runs due south between high rock walls: scramble down it and take the very first left it offers, and the rappel station comes into view as soon as the walls let you out, at roughly 6,000 ft. Parties miss it by carrying on too far down, or too far right, once the gully opens up.

The station is fixed and old — three rusty pitons tied together with a mass of aging webbing and a pair of aluminium rappel rings. Two ropes give a single 60 m rappel that clears the corniced lip and lands where the gully opens out and ends; a single 60 m rope halves that and leaves 30-40 m of very steep snow to downclimb, still fully exposed to whatever comes down the gully. Move to the side of the gully mouth once you are down so the next person cannot drop anything on you. A tag line is worth carrying for exactly that reason — it buys a quick rappel to a protected stance instead of a long spell standing in the fall line.

A second gully further along is an alter
wa_chair_peak_northeast_buttress.name: Northeast Buttress

wa_chair_peak_northwest_ridge.approach: Follow the East Face approach to the 'Thumbtack Rock' landmark, then head right up a grassy gully over the ridge toward the start of the Northwest Ridge.
wa_chair_peak_northwest_ridge.descent_text: From the true summit, traverse south across a series of false summits until reaching a tree rigged with rappel anchors at the second gully encountered heading east. Make multiple rappels down this gully to reach the East Face proper, then descend scree slopes back to Thumbtack Rock and the standard approach path.
wa_chair_peak_northwest_ridge.name: Northwest Ridge

wa_chair_peak_west_ridge.approach: From the Alpental lot, follow the standard Northeast Buttress approach to the base of that buttress, then keep traversing west beneath the north face on slabby terrain that can be snowy and glide-cracked in early season to reach the base of the route, roughly 2-2.5 hours from the parking area.
wa_chair_peak_west_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, descend via the standard south-side couloir, which funnels into the same narrow rappel gully used by the other Chair Peak routes; reported descent time is about 1-2 hours back to the Chair Peak basin.
wa_chair_peak_west_ridge.name: West Ridge

wa_chimney_rock_east_face_direct.approach: Same as the standard East Face: Pete Lake Trailhead (2,800 ft) via Pete Lake Trail/PCT and the Chimney Creek climber's path to high camp at Sunrise Knob (~4,600-4,800 ft).
wa_chimney_rock_east_face_direct.descent_text: Once the route rejoins the standard East Face partway up, descend as for that route: downclimb/rappel with a single rope, carrying spare webbing for old anchors.
wa_chimney_rock_east_face_direct.name: East Face Direct

wa_chimney_rock_west_face.approach: This route shares the same trailhead-to-basin approach as the East Face: from the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616, hike the Pete Lake Trail #1323 (~4 easy miles to Pete Lake, then ~2 more miles) to the Pacific Crest Trail junction, head north on the PCT about a mile to the Chimney Creek avalanche-path crossing, then leave the PCT and follow the climber's path (flagged/cairned, fords Chimney Creek and crosses several brushy ravines) up through Sunrise Knob (~4,650 ft, ~4-5 hrs from the trailhead) to the moraine and the bivy basin at the toe of the Chimney Glacier (~5,400 ft) — see the East Face route's approach text for full turn-by-turn detail on this shared stretch, and treat it as a 2-3 day car-to-car trip. Above camp, a wet, grubby gully through the rock band leads onto the upper Chimney Glacier; rope up, cross toward the gully below the notch between the central and south summits, and be ready to improvise around the moat at the foot of the rock, which gets worse later in the season. Water and camping options match the East Face approach: Pete Lake, the low Chimney Creek crossings, or melted glacier snow above the moraine.
wa_chimney_rock_west_face.descent_text: Descend the line of ascent. From the South Peak, return about 400 ft to the notch between the central and south summits, then follow the ledge system back down; the ledges are easy to pick out from above. Rappel the steeper, wet fourth-class steps on a single 60 m rope rather than downclimbing them. No fixed anchors are known on this line, so carry slings, cord and a few rap rings to build and leave your own. Cross the moat back onto the glacier, reverse the glacier and the gully through the rock band, and return to camp.
wa_chimney_rock_west_face.name: South Peak via East Gully

wa_east_face_6.approach: From the Pete Lake Trailhead off FR 4616 (elev. ~2,850 ft), follow the Pete Lake Trail #1323 west and north through open, nearly-flat forest along Cooper River/Lemah Meadow terrain — easy tread and wildflower meadows for about 4 miles to the south shore of Pete Lake, a popular first camp and reliable water source. Continue past the lake about a mile, through Lemah Meadow, to the Pacific Crest Trail junction and turn north onto the PCT. After about a mile of PCT travel, watch for a wide avalanche path with heavy blowdown crossing the trail near the confluence of Chimney Creek — this is the turnoff for the climb. Leave the PCT and work climber's-right across the avalanche debris to pick up a boot/climber's path on the true-right side of Chimney Creek (it starts roughly 20 yards inside the timber at an obvious logjam that serves as the creek crossing, and is marked intermittently with orange flagging and cairns). The path crosses three brushy ravines, and pushes through alder and vine maple before breaking into open moraine and a hanging basin — cairns mark the line through this stretch, which is the main route-finding crux of the approach. A rock buttress called Sunrise Knob (~4,650
wa_east_face_6.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line rather than continuing over the summit block. From the summit, rappel the three summit pitches back to the broad ledge below the tower (two rappels on a single rope; some parties make three), then traverse back through the notch/gully between the main and south summits (a short reversal of the ascent gully, Class 3-4 downclimbing over loose debris or snow/ice depending on season). Where the rock steepens near the base of the face, on the wet, lower-angle slabs just above the glacier, most parties make two rappels over these fourth-class steps using a single rope (a 50-60m/165ft rope is enough for each); anchors here are natural — slung horns and blocks rather than bolts — so carry cord/webbing to back up or replace old tat, especially early in the season. Below the raps, a final short third-class downclimb regains the bergschrund/moat crossing back onto the Chimney Glacier, then reverse the moraine and climber's path to Sunrise Knob and the Pete Lake Trail. Watch for loose rock/rockfall in the gully, wet slick rock on the fourth-class rappel steps, and crevasse/moat hazard back on the glacier.
wa_east_face_6.name: East Face

wa_accendo_lunae_lib_west_face_var.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), take the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain to Colchuck Lake — forest walking along Mountaineer Creek, a log-bridge crossing at 1.5 miles, turning left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, then a final boulder-moraine climb to the outlet (2.5-3 hours). Fill water here. Continue around the lake's west shore to its south end and onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min, exposed to wet-snow slips into July), then break climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Accendo Lunae — a linkup that starts on Let It Burn's line and finishes via a West Face variation — begins at the same point in the base gully as Let It Burn, on the wall's lower-left section, before diverging upward. Expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final scramble to the wall; rope up if uncertain.
wa_accendo_lunae_lib_west_face_var.descent_text: Because Accendo Lunae finishes by joining a West Face variation, it shares Colchuck Balanced Rock's standard summit descent: scramble class 3-4 around the right side of the true summit block (bypassing the balanced boulder) to the sandy scree/talus gully, then descend clockwise around the peak back to the base of the climbs (45 min-1hr). A short section near the top is sometimes eased with an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn on the east side (natural anchor) rather than downclimbed. No full rappel of the route line itself is needed.
wa_accendo_lunae_lib_west_face_var.name: Accendo Lunae (LiB/West Face Var.)

wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.approach: This is the approach/scramble route to the col above Colchuck Lake's east side, used to access objectives beyond Colchuck Balanced Rock (notably Dragontail Peak). Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road) and hike the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) and Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) 4 miles and 2,280 ft to the lake outlet (2.5-3 hours), the last reliable water. At the lake, take the left fork and stay high on the ridge, avoiding spur trails that drop to the water's edge. Continue to a small dam near the lake's north end and cross the outlet creek at or just below it; pick up the trail on the far side and follow it south roughly 100 yards to a slight clearing with boulders and talus on the left. Ascend the talus, angling slightly left into the woods, and negotiate a brief 3rd/4th-class rock step (using roots/branches as holds). From there the path climbs southward through open, cairned forest for about an hour to the col, which overlooks a boulder-strewn camp area with views of Dragontail and Colchuck peaks — about 2,500 ft above the lake, or roughly 4,600 ft of gain from the trailhead.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.descent_text: This is a hiking/scrambling approach line, not a technical climb, so descent is simply the reverse of the ascent: down through the open, cairned forest, back through the brief 3rd/4th-class rock step, down the talus to the clearing, back across the outlet creek near the small dam, and along the high ridge line back to the lakeshore trail and out to the Stuart Lake Trailhead. No rappelling is involved. The 3rd/4th-class step and the talus above the dam are the main hazards — loose rock and awkward footing, worse if wet or descending in the dark.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_col_east_lake_.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock Col (East Lake Side Approch)

wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601, off Icicle Creek Road outside Leavenworth; NW Forest Pass required). Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) about 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge around the 1.5-mile mark, to the signed junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) splits left. Continue on #1599A, crossing Mountaineer Creek again on a second log bridge, then climb increasingly steep, rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain from the trailhead, roughly 1:45-2:00 for a fit party with a rack). From the lake there are two ways into the west basin below Colchuck Balanced Rock (CBR): the shorter northern line crosses the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follows a climbers' path across a timbered hillside directly into the cirque below the west face (about an hour, plus roughly 20-25 minutes of boulder-hopping to the actual base); the longer southern/Aasgard option follows the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, cuts north through a band of slide alder (look for cairns), then climbs the leftmost gully about 1,000 ft to its top before contouring east on an easy
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.descent_text: Descend the same way you climbed the upper pitches: from the top, scramble to a slung horn on the east side of the summit block and make one roughly 30-meter (about 100 ft) rappel — a single rope is sufficient, though some parties extend it with a doubled 60m for a lower touchdown. The anchor is a natural horn wrapped in webbing rather than bolts, so back it up or add your own sling if it looks tired; it sees heavy traffic and gets re-slung periodically. From the rappel's end, downclimb/scramble sandy scree and talus, working rightward (clockwise around the peak, roughly south then west) back into the basin and to your pack stash at the base of the west face — about 45 minutes to an hour car-to-base-equivalent. Some parties skip the rappel entirely and downclimb the same easy scree/snow line if conditions allow, since the terrain below the horn is low-angle. No further rappels are needed; this is the standard, single-rappel descent used for the West Face, The Scoop, and other CBR lines that top out on the summit block.
wa_colchuck_balanced_rock_west_face.name: West Face

wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FS Road 7601, Eightmile Road, ~3,400 ft — reached via Icicle Road/FS 76 from Leavenworth, roughly 8.4 miles, then FS 7601 another 3.8 miles), follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 south along Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles/1,100 ft of gain to the signed fork; take the right/south branch (Colchuck Lake Trail) and climb steep switchbacks through boulders for another 1.6 miles/1,100 ft to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, about 4 miles and 2,200 ft from the trailhead — a popular, often-permitted overnight zone in the Enchantments quota area, so many parties camp here rather than pushing to the summit car-to-car). Colchuck Lake is the last reliable water. From the lake, follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail and climb talus (or snow early season) directly up the basin toward the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600–6,800 ft — this is the standard, moderate line up the peak (3rd class/mod. snow) and doubles as the descent for the other two routes here. The glacier itself is not significantly crevassed but is frequently icy by mid-to-late season, so crampons and an axe (and a rope if any crevasses/mo
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.descent_text: This is a walk-off — no rappels. Reverse the ascent line: descend the glacier (staying climber's left, away from the thin crevasse zone that has opened as the glacier has retreated) and back down the lateral moraine to Colchuck Lake, then follow the Colchuck Lake Trail and Stuart Lake Trail back to the trailhead. In early season with good snow cover, much of the glacier and the upper trail basin can be glissaded, which many parties use to save time — but glissading here carries the usual runout/collision risk of any steep snow slope, so glissade only with a self-arrest-ready ice axe and clear runout. By afternoon on warm days the glacier softens considerably (postholing, wet-slide potential on any residual snow slopes), so climbers doing this as a long day often aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon.
wa_colchuck_peak_colchuck_glacier.name: Colchuck Glacier

wa_colchuck_peak_holsten_hilden.approach: Hike the Stuart Lake Trail to Colchuck Lake, then continue to the base of the Colchuck Glacier/moraine below Colchuck's northeast face. The route starts right of the Northeast Couloir: two 60m pitches of AI3 ice gain the initial couloir, followed by several hundred feet of 50-60 degree snow trending up-left, then unconsolidated snow over rock, a short traverse left into an M6 chimney, and a final steep snow/rock band to the notch on the north ridge crest.
wa_colchuck_peak_holsten_hilden.descent_text: From the top of the route, join the standard East Route line and descend the Colchuck Glacier back toward Colchuck Col and Colchuck Lake, then follow the approach trail out.
wa_colchuck_peak_holsten_hilden.name: Holsten-Hilden

wa_colchuck_peak_north_buttress_couloir.approach: Follow the shared Colchuck Peak approach: from Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road ~8.4 mi to FR 7601, then FR 7601 ~3.7 mi to Stuart Lake Trailhead; hike the Stuart Lake/Colchuck Lake Trail (~4-4.5 mi, ~2,200 ft gain) to Colchuck Lake. From the lake's far (south) side, hike up and gain the moraine, follow it to the right, and drop into the couloir — it is the first major gully reached rising out of the toe of the Colchuck Glacier's moraine.
wa_colchuck_peak_north_buttress_couloir.descent_text: Descend the backside of the mountain onto the Colchuck Glacier and follow its standard route and the moraine back to Colchuck Lake; in soft, late-day snow this descent has been reported as slow and exhausting.
wa_colchuck_peak_north_buttress_couloir.name: North Buttress Couloir

wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FS Road 7601 (Eightmile Road), elevation ~3,400 ft — in early season when Eightmile Road is gated/snowed in, tack on roughly 4 additional miles of road walking/skiing from the Bridge Creek Campground area on Icicle Road. From the trailhead, follow Stuart Lake Trail #1599 south along Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles and 1,100 ft of gain to the signed junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail forks left; the Stuart Lake Trail continues straight to Stuart Lake/Colchuck Pass and is not your route. Climb the steep, rooty switchbacks of the Colchuck Lake Trail through boulder fields for another 1.6 miles and 1,100 ft to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4 miles and 2,200 ft from the car) — this is the only reliable water source below the basin, and it's your last easy resupply. Follow the trail and boot path along the lake's west shore to the inlet at the south end (~5 miles in). Leave the maintained trail here and ascend talus, heather benches, or lingering snow (highly season-dependent) up the basin toward the toe of the Colchuck Glacier at roughly 6,600–6,800 ft. Rather than heading up-glacier toward Colchuck/Banshee Col (that's the Colchuck Glac
wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.descent_text: Standard descent is the walk-off: from the summit, traverse/downclimb to the Colchuck–Dragontail col (Colchuck Col, also called Banshee Pass) and descend the Colchuck Glacier's east/true-right lobe back to the basin above Colchuck Lake, then reverse the approach trail — the same line used to descend the Colchuck Glacier route. This is the recommended way down; reversing through the Northeast Couloir itself is discouraged because of loose rock in the entry gully and awkward mixed downclimbing. That said, some parties (particularly ski descents or parties that got benighted) do reverse the couloir instead of the full glacier walk-off: accounts describe downclimbing back to the top of the upper rock band, then either downclimbing it (not recommended) or making a single ~50m rappel off a natural anchor (you'll likely need to build one from boulders/slings — nothing fixed is documented) down to a ledge system on the southeast face; from there, a gully just east of the couloir's top can be down-climbed or rappelled with two or three single-strand 30m raps (again on natural/rigged anchors) to reach easier snow slopes, from which you continue down into the basin. Treat this as an emergency
wa_colchuck_peak_northeast_couloir.name: Northeast Couloir

wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.approach: Start at Hannegan Trailhead (3,100 ft) at the end of Ruth Creek Road (FR 32). Take the Hannegan Pass Trail roughly 4 miles and ~2,500 ft of gain up through subalpine forest and meadow to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft). From the pass, drop off the north side on the Chilliwack River Trail into the Chilliwack River valley — this loses most of the elevation just gained and is the start of a long valley traverse. The trail passes Copper Creek Camp (~9 mi) and U.S. Cabin Camp (~12 mi); expect brushy tread near U.S. Cabin Camp and, in blowdown years, stretches of downed timber (one trip report logged roughly two hours to move 1.5 miles through fallen trunks and limbs beyond the cable-car crossing). Cross the Chilliwack River on the hand-pulled cable car (a mandatory, somewhat exposed crossing — the river is not reliably fordable). Beyond the crossing, pick up the Brush Creek Trail, which climbs steadily (generally in better condition, with only scattered blowdown) to Whatcom Pass (5,206 ft, ~17 mi in). From Whatcom Camp near the pass, leave maintained trail and traverse cross-country below Whatcom Peak's northeast flank via the Whatcom Glacier to Perfect Pass (about 4.5 hours and 1,750 ft of ga
wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.descent_text: Reverse the climbing route from the summit rather than continuing over the north ridge. Down-climb the loose, exposed class 4-5 summit ridge and ledges just south of the true summit using running belays and gear placements — this terrain is horribly loose, so treat every hold as suspect and keep the rope short between placements. At the top of the crux headwall, make one single-strand rappel down the ~10-ft near-vertical crack (roughly 5.8+ or 5.2/A1); a single 30-40m rope reaches the ledge below. Continue down and along the loose class 4-5 ledges around the north ridge's pinnacles to a rock horn draped with old rappel slings (do not trust weathered fixed tat — back it up with your own cord); from this horn, make two rappels on doubled ropes (the one party to record this descent joined a 40m and a 30m 6.9mm alpine rope) to reach an exit ledge above the couloir — a single 60m rope doubled, or two 30m ropes, works as a substitute. From the exit ledge, down-climb the 40-45° northwest snow couloir, placing snow pickets or flukes as protection if conditions are firm or icy, back to the saddle just north of the peak and down to camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine. From camp, revers
wa_crooked_thumb_peak_south_route.name: South Route

wa_davis_peak_nc_north_face.approach: From Diablo, take the Stetattle Creek trail about 2 mi, drop about 200 ft to ford the creek opposite Davis Peak, then bushwhack and scramble a Class 3-4 rib, roping up for slabby sections, through slide alder above the cliffs to flat ground at the toe of the glacier, about 4,000 ft. Expect roughly eight or nine hours from the road. The whole Stetattle Creek Trail has been closed until further notice for post-fire hazards (falling dead trees and unstable ground); check its status with North Cascades National Park before a trip.
wa_davis_peak_nc_north_face.descent_text:
The northeast face has no easy retreat; descend the south side, which is long and unpleasant but walkable.

From the top of the couloir at about 6,700 ft, rappel from pitons onto the SE ridge (or continue up the ridge to the 7,054 ft summit first if time allows). Descend the south side following the South Slope and Ridge route in reverse: down the ridge crest, past the 5,720+ ft saddle, over or around Point 5872, and then straight down the sustained trackless forest of the south slope to the highway.

Daylight is the key. Descending the upper 1,500 ft in the light avoids the cliff bands, and the rappels off trees that come with getting them wrong. The forest below is thick, but the right line has no cliffs and little slide alder; allow about four hours from the top of the timber to the road. The timber is dense enough to hide landmarks, so navigate by compass to avoid ending up in Stetattle Creek.

You finish at the Gorge Creek bridge, about four highway miles from the parking in Diablo, so arrange a shuttle car.
wa_davis_peak_nc_north_face.name: Northeast Face Couloir

wa_davis_peak_nc_south_slope_and_ridge.approach: There is no trailhead in the usual sense — you step off the highway into the forest. Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of Newhalem near milepost 123, or about the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp turn at the east end of the bridge. There are parking lots at each end; the east lot is signed for motorhomes and oversize vehicles, so park at the west lot. Elevation here is 1,096 ft, and there are accessible restrooms and a short interpretive trail to the Gorge Creek Falls viewpoint. Walk across the bridge to its east end, go a few feet farther east, cross the highway, and pick the easiest place to start uphill into the woods. That is the whole approach: the route and the approach are the same thing from here, 6,000 vertical feet of it. Round trip is about 6.2 miles with roughly 6,000 ft of gain in three miles. Carry water. The slope is south-facing and dry once the snow is gone, and there is no reliable source between the highway and the snowfields high on the mountain. In late spring, snowmelt on the route solves this and simultaneously suppresses the brush, which is why that window is the usual recomm
wa_davis_peak_nc_south_slope_and_ridge.descent_text:
Descend the south ridge crest directly rather than reversing the east-basin variation. The step that drops into the saddle looks formidably steep from camp — steep enough that at least one party detoured around it on the way up — but it is climbed down easily, with all the ledges you need. Below the saddle, retrace your line through Point 5872 and the open slopes.

The work is in the forest. Stay on the line you came up: the cliff bands near 2,400 ft and 2,800 ft need to be turned on the correct side, and getting them wrong means rappelling off trees. Slabs low on the mountain are covered in slippery moss, and one party reported a 3rd-class chimney with an awkward move below it as the crux of the descent. Expect deadfall fields. Total descent time is about 4.1 hours from the summit for a fit party moving well, and every account calls it brutal on the knees.

If you are descending this route after climbing the northeast face, the strong advice from the party that did it is to get the top 1,500 ft done in daylight — that is what lets you avoid the cliff bands — and to carry a compass, because the timber is dense enough to hide the dam lights and a drift to the east puts you in Stetat
wa_davis_peak_nc_south_slope_and_ridge.name: South Slope and Ridge

wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.approach: From the Downey Creek Campground trailhead (~1,450 ft) on Suiattle River Road (FR 26), take the Downey Creek Trail #768, staying on the east bank of Downey Creek through old-growth forest. The trail is rough and lightly maintained — expect brush, downed timber, and washed-out sections; a footlog or ford may be needed at Bachelor Creek (~6.5 mi in), which has been scoured by past avalanches that swept debris across the valley and buried sections of trail. Beyond Bachelor Creek the trail climbs steeply out of the valley toward Cub Lake, gaining roughly 4,000+ ft from the trailhead; this stretch crosses open avalanche paths below Spire Point that should be assessed for stability in early-season snow. Camp is typically made in meadows southeast of Cub Lake (~5,300 ft) or, better positioned for summit day, up on the ridge above at ~6,200 ft (add ~1 hr from the lake). Reported car-to-camp time is 9-11 hours given the distance, brush, and elevation gain — budget this as a genuine multi-day approach, not a day hike-in. From high camp, a boot path crosses the south ridge toward Spire Point, then the route drops ~200 ft and traverses cross-country (roughly 80° bearing) below cliff bands, ove
wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the rock arête (~500 ft) back to the notch at 8,560 ft, then down the snow slope (~300 ft) onto the Dome Glacier, and back down-glacier along the ascent track to the base of the climb, retracing the cross-country traverse back to high camp. The rock arête itself is narrow, exposed, and largely featureless — many parties belay or fix a handline/rappel for at least part of it rather than downclimbing unroped, especially in the upper section near the summit. The more consequential technical step is typically the bergschrund on the Dome Glacier below the notch: depending on the season and how open the 'schrund is, parties commonly need one rappel (single 60m rope reported sufficient) to get down past it safely, building an anchor from snow pickets, a buried deadman, or a v-thread in firm ice — there are no fixed/bolted anchors on this remote, seldom-traveled route. In a low-snow year or if the bergschrund is well-bridged, this step may be downclimbable with no rappel at all, so treat the rappel as conditions-dependent rather than fixed. Below the glacier, re-cross the loose/polished traverse back toward Cub Lake camp with care, then descend th
wa_dome_peak_dome_glacier.name: Dome Glacier

wa_full_tilt_tempest_wall_free_version.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), take the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) to Colchuck Lake — 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek at 1.5 miles, turning left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, then a boulder-moraine finish to the outlet (2.5-3 hours, last water). Continue around the lake's west shore to the boulder field at its south end and onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min, holds wet snow into July), then cut climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Full Tilt — the free version of the Tempest Wall's aid line(s) — starts a few hundred feet down the gully to the right of the West Face's start, on Grade III terrain. Expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final scramble to the wall.
wa_full_tilt_tempest_wall_free_version.descent_text: Full Tilt climbs the Tempest Wall and finishes over the top. Continue to the summit ridge and use Colchuck Balanced Rock’s standard walk-off: class 3-4 scrambling around the summit block to a sandy scree gully, with one optional rappel of about 30 m off a slung horn on the east side, then clockwise around the peak to the base, about 50 minutes. The Tipping Point, on the same wall, has a bolted two-rappel bail line from its Sky Lounge belay into the approach gully; plan on the walk-off rather than rappelling Full Tilt itself.
wa_full_tilt_tempest_wall_free_version.name: Full Tilt (Tempest Wall Free Version)

wa_leche_la_vaca.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599): gentle forest walking along Mountaineer Creek for 1.5 miles to a log-bridge crossing, then left onto the Colchuck Lake fork at the Lake Stuart Trail junction (about 2.25 miles), then a final boulder-moraine push to the lake outlet — about 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, 2.5-3 hours. Top off water here, the last reliable source. Continue around toward the lake's south/east shore onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining steep talus and heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; a slope that holds wet snow into July and has produced serious slips). Cut climber's-left off the Aasgard trail through a dense slide-alder/heather band (15-20 minutes of real bushwhacking) to the base of the gully system below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Leche La Vaca starts in this same base gully area on the left side of the wall, near Scarface; the final approach scramble to the wall is loose 3rd/4th class terrain. Figure 3.5-4 hours car-to-base overall.
wa_leche_la_vaca.descent_text: Leche La Vaca's fifth pitch, a long 4th-class to low-5th traverse, ends at the summit block — from there it shares Colchuck Balanced Rock's standard walk-off: scramble class 3-4 around the right side of the true summit block (staying off the balanced boulder itself) down to a broad sandy scree/talus gully, descending clockwise back around the peak to the base of the climbs (45 min-1hr). A short step near the top of this descent is sometimes eased with an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn (natural anchor) on the east side rather than downclimbing it — treat this as optional, not mandatory. No full rappel of the route itself is required.
wa_leche_la_vaca.name: Leche La Vaca

wa_let_it_burn.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) to Colchuck Lake — forest along Mountaineer Creek, a log-bridge crossing at 1.5 miles, left onto the Colchuck Lake fork at the Lake Stuart Trail junction (about 2.25 miles), then a boulder-moraine finish to the outlet (about 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain). Fill water here — it's the last source. Cross the outlet and continue toward the lake's south/east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake, then cut left through dense brush to the obvious base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. From the gully, scramble up a 3rd-class ramp to the actual base of the technical climbing. A documented approach for this route took about 3 hours 47 minutes trailhead-to-base, matching the 3.5-4 hour estimate.
wa_let_it_burn.descent_text: From the top of the route, most parties make an optional ~30m rappel down the south/southwest side off a slung horn (natural anchor, not bolted) — this step can be bypassed entirely if the party avoids the summit block area. After the rappel (or bypass), descend scree or snow rightward (clockwise around the peak) back to the base of the climb. A documented descent took about 50 minutes from the top of the route to the base, plus roughly 3 hours 5 minutes hiking back out to the trailhead. This is the same walk-off shared by the West Face and The Scoop. Loose rock on the scree gully is the main hazard, especially with parties above; watch footing on wet or snow-covered sections early in the season.
wa_let_it_burn.name: Let it Burn

wa_milk_n_honey.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), hike the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) — 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, forest along Mountaineer Creek with a log-bridge crossing at 1.5 miles, bearing left at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, finishing on a boulder moraine to the outlet (2.5-3 hours). Fill water here, the last source. Follow the trail along the lake's west shore to its southeast end and take the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail up steep talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; holds wet snow into July), then break climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully system below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Milk n' Honey (5.11) sits in the same general wall area as The Scoop and Rikki Tikki Tavi, toward the right side of the formation; expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final scramble to the base. Figure 3.5-4 hours car-to-base.
wa_milk_n_honey.descent_text: Milk n' Honey tops out on Colchuck Balanced Rock's upper wall and, like its neighbors, most likely shares the standard summit descent: class 3-4 scrambling around the right side of the true summit block to a sandy scree/talus gully, descended clockwise back around the peak to the base of the climbs (45 min-1hr), with a short step near the top sometimes eased by an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn (natural anchor) on the east side. No full rappel of the route is confirmed to be required.
wa_milk_n_honey.name: Milk n' Honey

wa_northeast_buttress_4.approach: Approach as for the Colchuck Glacier route: Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FS 7601/Eightmile Road, ~3,400 ft) via Stuart Lake Trail #1599 (2.5 mi/1,100 ft to the fork) and then the Colchuck Lake Trail (1.6 mi/1,100 ft of switchbacks) to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4 mi/2,200 ft in) — the last reliable water. From the lake's east-shore boot path, continue to the inlet at the south end, then climb talus/snow up the basin to the toe of the Colchuck Glacier (~6,600–6,800 ft). Rather than continuing to the col, angle up and across the glacier's true-right margin toward Colchuck Peak's northeast side to reach the base of the buttress itself; parties describe crossing the moat via a snow bridge or snow block that varies season to season and can be the technical crux of the approach in a lean year — some parties rope up for this short glacier crossing. Given the length of the route (14+ pitches) and the multi-stage approach, most parties start pre-dawn (some parties make 1:30 a.m. trailhead starts to be racking up at the base by first light) or camp at Colchuck Lake and do the climb as a long day from there. There is no water above Colchuck Lake, so carry what you need for the full push.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.descent_text: This is a walk-off, not a rappel descent: from the summit plateau, downclimb/traverse to Colchuck–Dragontail Col (Colchuck Col/Banshee Pass) and descend the Colchuck Glacier's east/true-right lobe — the same standard line used to descend the Colchuck Glacier route — back into the basin above Colchuck Lake, then follow the boot path and trail out. Staying on the glacier's margin (rather than its center) is the better choice for firmer footing and to avoid the worst of the moraine/talus below; glissading the lower snow when it's in is common. This descent consistently takes several hours on its own (roughly 5 hours summit-to-car for one party) after a long climb, so plan for a full-value day; the crux hazard on the way down is fatigue-driven routefinding through the moraine/talus and re-crossing the moat near the col, not technical terrain. No rappelling is reported anywhere on the descent.
wa_northeast_buttress_4.name: Northeast Buttress

wa_nw_ridge_2.approach: Hike the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) and the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599.1) from the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road) — 4 miles and 2,280 ft gain, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge at 1.5 miles and staying left at the Lake Stuart Trail junction — to reach Colchuck Lake (2.5-3 hours). Unlike the west-side routes, the NW Ridge is approached from the east side of the lake: work around the eastern shoreline/talus to the base of the obvious gully that splits toward the notch above Jabberwocky Tower, the granite spire between the lake and Colchuck Balanced Rock. Ascend this gully (loose in spots, rope-up terrain for the upper section) to the notch, then move onto class-3 ground on the NW Ridge proper before the climbing begins. One documented ascent clocked roughly 4,760 ft of total gain and a 12-hour car-to-car day, consistent with the route's ~18.5 km round-trip distance.
wa_nw_ridge_2.descent_text: From the ridge's high point (below the exposed summit boulder problem, which most parties do not attempt due to thin protection), descend via a single ~25m rappel down the east face off a fixed anchor — a natural sling/horn setup rather than bolts, so inspect it before committing. After the rappel, scramble down talus and broken rock slopes, contouring around to a saddle on the south side, back past Jabberwocky Tower, and down to Colchuck Lake to rejoin the standard hike-out. Loose rock and route-finding through the talus are the main descent hazards; this is not a walk in fading light without a headlamp given the boulder-hopping involved.
wa_nw_ridge_2.name: NW Ridge

wa_rikki_tikki_tavi.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), follow the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) to Colchuck Lake — 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek at 1.5 miles, turning left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the Stuart Lake Trail junction, finishing with a boulder-moraine climb to the outlet (2.5-3 hours, last reliable water). Continue around the west shore to the lake's south end and onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; holds wet snow into July, with a real slip-and-fall history), then cut climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully below Colchuck Balanced Rock. Rikki Tikki Tavi (5.11, 5 pitches) sits to the right of The Scoop on the wall; expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final scramble to the base. Total trailhead-to-base time is around 3.5-4 hours.
wa_rikki_tikki_tavi.descent_text: Rikki Tikki Tavi's five pitches top out in the upper-wall area shared with The Scoop and Milk n' Honey, and most likely shares Colchuck Balanced Rock's standard summit descent: class 3-4 scrambling around the right side of the true summit block down to a sandy scree/talus gully, descended clockwise back around the peak to the base of the climbs (45 min-1hr), with a short step near the top sometimes eased by an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn (natural anchor) on the east side. The Scoop, immediately to its left, is noted as having natural tree/horn anchors that allow rappelling the route itself as an alternative, which may also be an option here given the shared rock character.
wa_rikki_tikki_tavi.name: Rikki Tikki Tavi

wa_scarface_3.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road), follow the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599) — 4 miles, 2,280 ft gain, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge at 1.5 miles, bearing left at the Lake Stuart Trail junction, finishing with a boulder-moraine climb to the outlet (2.5-3 hours). Top off water here. Head toward the lake's south/east side onto the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, gaining talus/heather to about 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min, watch for wet snow into July), then cut climber's-left through dense slide-alder/heather brush (15-20 minutes) to the base gully system. Scarface climbs the gully just left of the West Face route's start; this terrain is very loose and exposed, so extra care with rope-up/spacing is warranted through the final approach scramble. Total trailhead-to-base time runs about 3.5-4 hours, in line with neighboring routes.
wa_scarface_3.descent_text: Scarface tops out near the other West Face-area routes and shares Colchuck Balanced Rock's standard summit descent: class 3-4 scrambling around the right side of the true summit block (avoiding the balanced boulder) down to a sandy scree/talus gully, descended clockwise back around the peak to the base (45 min-1hr). A short section near the top is sometimes eased with an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn on the east side (natural anchor) instead of downclimbing. No full rappel of the route itself is required under normal conditions.
wa_scarface_3.name: Scarface

wa_the_balanced_rock.approach: This is not a ground-up approach — 'The Balanced Rock' is the short V1 boulder problem on top of the balanced summit block of Colchuck Balanced Rock itself, at roughly 8,240 ft. It's reached only after climbing one of the peak's technical routes to the summit ridge (most commonly the West Face or Let It Burn, both approached via the Stuart Lake Trailhead/Colchuck Lake Trail and the Aasgard Pass climbers' trail — see those routes for the full trailhead-to-wall approach, roughly 3.5-4 hours). From the summit ridge, a short 3rd/4th-class scramble around the true high point leads to the base of the balanced boulder, where the problem climbs the exposed south-east crimpy arête, about 12 ft tall.
wa_the_balanced_rock.descent_text: There is no rope or rappel involved in the boulder problem itself — downclimbing the same crimpy arête is described as 'the crux,' and protection notes on the route simply warn 'don't fall,' since it's exposed above the summit block with no gear placements. After downclimbing, descend via whichever route's standard summit walk-off you used to reach the top — typically class 3-4 scrambling around the summit block to a sandy scree gully, with an optional single ~30m rappel off a slung horn on the east side (natural anchor) — back down to the base of the climbs.
wa_the_balanced_rock.name: The Balanced Rock

wa_the_scoop_2.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (NF-7601 off Icicle Creek Road; NW Forest Pass required) and follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) roughly 2.25 miles, crossing Mountaineer Creek on a log bridge near the 1.5-mile mark, to the junction where the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) branches left. Stay on #1599A across a second Mountaineer Creek log crossing and up steepening, rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake (about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain, roughly 1:45-2:00 hiking). From the lake, reach Colchuck Balanced Rock's west basin either via the shorter northern line — cross the lake's outlet below the small dam at the north end and follow a climbers' path across timbered hillside straight into the cirque (about an hour, plus ~20-25 minutes boulder-hopping the talus to the actual base) — or the longer southern/Aasgard line, following the lakeshore path counter-clockwise toward the Aasgard Pass slopes, cutting north through a slide-alder band (cairned) into the leftmost gully, climbing that ~1,000 ft to its top, then contouring east on an easy path into the basin (1.5-2 hours, more gain but no ford). The Scoop starts in the basin to the right of the West Face and the Tempest, left of Rikki Ti
wa_the_scoop_2.descent_text: Parties who top out can use CBR's standard descent shared with the West Face: a single 30 m rappel east from a slung horn, then scree or snow clockwise around the peak to the base. The alternative, which avoids that loose ground, is to rappel the route itself: with two 60m ropes tied together, descend via a sequence of natural anchors — slung trees and horns down the crack systems below Launch Ledge — there are no bolts or fixed gear anywhere on the route, by design, so you are relying entirely on what you find or build (extra slings/cord are worth carrying). Watch for rope-snag risk in the corner systems on the crux Scoop pitch and loose rock low in the gully system if you bail before topping out. No count of rappels down the route itself is published; the route is about 1,000 ft over 10 pitches, so expect a long series, and be ready to build or equalize a natural anchor if a station looks marginal.
wa_the_scoop_2.name: The Scoop

wa_the_tempest.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (FS Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road, ~8.5 miles from Leavenworth) and follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599). The first 1.5 miles climb gently through forest alongside Mountaineer Creek to a log-bridge crossing; about a mile past that, fork left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A). The final push switchbacks up a boulder moraine to the Colchuck Lake outlet — about 4 miles and 2,280 ft of gain, 2.5-3 hours at a steady pace. This is the last reliable water; fill up here. Work around toward the lake's south/east side and pick up the cairned Aasgard Pass climbers' trail, following it up steep talus/heather to roughly 400 ft above the lake (30-40 min; this slope holds snow into July and has a real slip-and-fall history). Break off climber's-left through a band of dense slide alder and heather — the brushy crux of the hike-in, 15-20 minutes — to the base of the gully system below Colchuck Balanced Rock's main wall. The Tempest begins at the center of the face, below the long bulge/roof, roughly mid-way along the base — a bit right of the West Face's gully start. Expect loose 3rd/4th-class rock in the final approach scramble; many
wa_the_tempest.descent_text: The Tempest was originally aided by its first ascensionists and later freed ground-to-summit; most parties who top out on the summit ridge use the standard Colchuck Balanced Rock walk-off: class 3-4 scrambling around the right (south) side of the true summit block to a broad sandy/scree gully, with a short step near the top sometimes eased by a single ~30m (100ft) rappel to the east off a sling around a horn (natural anchor, not bolted) — many parties simply downclimb this step instead. From there it's a loose scree/talus descent, clockwise around the peak, back to the base of the route (45 min-1hr). Parties who don't want the loose summit scramble — or who are bailing partway — instead rappel the route itself, tree-to-tree on natural anchors; the route can also be rappelled with two 60m ropes, avoiding the loose walk-off. Over the route's ~9 pitches (roughly 1,000+ ft) that works out to somewhere around 7-9 tree-anchor rappels with double 60m ropes. Watch for rope-snag risk in trees and loose blocks on this alpine wall either way.
wa_the_tempest.name: The Tempest

wa_the_tipping_point.approach: Standard Colchuck Balanced Rock approach via Colchuck Lake and the Aasgard Pass gully; the route is to the left of Let It Burn and the West Face.
wa_the_tipping_point.descent_text: After topping out via Let it Burn’s upper pitches, take the standard summit descent: an optional single rappel of about 30 m from a slung horn, then scree or snow clockwise around the peak back to the base. To retreat from the lower half instead, rappel to the Sky Lounge, the two-bolt ledge atop pitch 3, stopping first at the Kerwin’s Crack anchor if your rope does not reach it in one; from the Sky Lounge, two rappels of about 40 m each return to the approach gully. Those need two ropes or an 80 m rope; a single 60 m rope folded double reaches only 30 m.
wa_the_tipping_point.name: The Tipping Point
